title: Trained as a printer but shut out by segregated unions
summary: Wilson graduated Tuskegee in 1928 as a printer but could not get Detroit newspaper work because the printers' union was white only; he lists segregated musicians' locals.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: But there was one serious flaw. Now, for instance, in my own case, I came out of Tuskegee, I graduated high school there in 1928. And with excellent -- as a printer.

Now after I came north, well, I went to school one year in a one year college at Talledega where I took a music major. But the disadvantage of the schooling at Tuskegee, I was not able to use it when I came north because I went to Detroit, and all my printing knowledge couldn't be used because I didn't belong to the union -- and the printers union was white only. Because I applied for jobs, like I was qualified to work on the Detroit News or the Detroit Free Press -- I could linotype at the government specified minimum of a professional linotype operator; but I couldn't get a job because of the segregated union.
But that was the fault of the system, though, not that of Booker T. Washington's teaching, because he had you prepared.
Yeah, I was prepared -- yeah, but the dead end was reached though, with the segregation in the unions -- and as you know, in our musicians union, in those
days, they were all segregated except maybe Local 5 in Detroit, I think, was never segregated -- and 802 in New York.

But you know, Chicago, we had 208 and 410, and right now in Boston, you have 9535 -- they're all amalgamated now, but oh, in those days, they were all segregated except New York, the big cities like New York and Detroit -- they were the only ones that weren't segregated.
